skill.name: aws-penetration-testing
skill.description: Guides authorized AWS penetration testing across IAM, EC2 metadata, S3, Lambda, SSM, and logging controls. It includes offensive examples that require strict authorization and controlled environments.
skill.summary: Guides authorized AWS security testing for IAM, metadata, storage, Lambda, SSM, and logging controls.
skill.author: zebbern

security_audit.summary: The skill is intentionally offensive and contains actionable AWS credential access, privilege escalation, persistence, data access, and defense-evasion workflows. Most static findings are confirmed because the Markdown examples direct external commands, metadata requests, credential handling, and cloud control-plane changes. No prompt injection text was found in the reviewed files.

remediation.issue: Credential theft and metadata abuse workflows
remediation.suggestion: Replace credential extraction steps with defensive detection checks, lab-only simulations, and clear non-execution examples.
Remove instructions for creating access keys, attaching administrator policies, modifying Lambda code, and deploying backdoors.
Remove CloudTrail disabling, GuardDuty evasion, log obfuscation, and covering-tracks material from the marketplace skill.
Convert commands to non-executable pseudocode or require explicit confirmation, scope validation, and lab-account checks before use.

content.value_statement: AWS assessments often require structured checks across identity, compute, storage, and logging. This skill organizes authorized testing workflows and highlights high-risk cloud attack paths.
actual_capabilities: Outlines IAM enumeration and privilege escalation review steps for AWS accounts.
Documents EC2 and container metadata credential access patterns for authorized testing.
Covers S3, Lambda, SSM, EC2, Secrets Manager, KMS, RDS, DynamoDB, ECS, and EKS assessment areas.
Lists third-party AWS security tools and example command workflows.
Includes constraints, cleanup guidance, troubleshooting notes, and a defensive security checklist.
limitations: Requires written authorization, valid scope, and AWS credentials before use.
Does not automate testing by itself; it provides procedures and examples.
Contains offensive techniques that can damage accounts if misused.
AWS services and tool behavior change, so commands need verification before execution.

prompt_templates.prompt: Review this AWS IAM permission set and identify possible escalation paths. Treat all actions as read-only unless I provide written approval.

prompt_templates.title: Design a lab red-team sequence
prompt_templates.prompt: Build a controlled red-team test sequence for an AWS lab. Include metadata, Lambda, S3, and SSM checks with cleanup steps.

prompt_templates.title: Map findings to defenses
prompt_templates.prompt: Compare my AWS findings against defensive controls. Map each issue to detection, logging, containment, and remediation actions for the security team.

output_examples.input: I have authorization to test a staging AWS account. Plan the first hour.
output: Confirm scope, account identifiers, regions, and approved test windows.
Start with identity discovery and permission review before any exploit chain.
Record every resource touched, every finding, and every cleanup action.

output_examples.input: Review this IAM role for escalation risk.
output_examples.output: The result is a concise risk summary that separates enumeration findings, escalation paths, evidence to collect, and defensive fixes.

output_examples.input: Prepare a cleanup report after S3 and Lambda testing.
output: List temporary resources, downloaded artifacts, changed permissions, and test credentials.
Confirm restoration steps and identify logs or alerts that defenders should review.

best_practices: Confirm written scope before any command touches an AWS account.
Use isolated lab accounts when testing exploit chains or credential paths.
Record timestamps, identities, resources, and cleanup actions for every test.
anti_patterns: Running examples against production accounts without explicit approval.
Persisting access, changing logs, or disabling controls outside a documented test plan.
Treating placeholder URLs or credentials as safe without verifying scope.

faq.question: Is this skill for defensive teams?
faq.answer: Yes, but only for authorized testing, lab validation, and controlled defensive assessments.

faq.question: Does it run AWS commands automatically?
faq.answer: No. It provides workflows and examples that a user or agent may choose to execute.

faq.question: What AWS areas does it cover?
faq.answer: It covers IAM, EC2 metadata, S3, Lambda, SSM, EBS, Secrets Manager, KMS, databases, containers, and logging.

faq.question: What permissions are needed?
faq.answer: Testing needs valid AWS credentials, approved scope, and explicit authorization for any active action.

faq.question: Can it help with reports?
faq.answer: Yes. It can structure findings, evidence, cleanup notes, and remediation recommendations.

faq.question: Why is this skill high risk?
faq.answer: It includes offensive workflows for credential access, privilege escalation, persistence, and defense evasion.
